q: `pub trait Provider: Send + Sync` (base.rs:464) — the colon means:
options: Supertrait bounds: implementing types must also be Send and Sync
Provider inherits from Send and Sync as structs
Send/Sync are methods Provider must implement
The trait is only usable in async code
explanation: Traits aren't structs; there's no struct inheritance here.
Send and Sync are auto traits, not methods.
The bounds are about thread-safety capability, not async syntax.

q: Why does `complete()` in the Provider trait have a default body (collecting `stream`)?
options: New providers ship by implementing one method; the boilerplate is shared
Defaults make trait methods optional to call
Rust requires half of each trait to have bodies
It forces every provider to buffer its stream
explanation: Default bodies still exist unless overridden; callers always can call them.
No such requirement exists in Rust.
Buffering is the default behavior — overridable when it hurts.

q: `Box<dyn Provider>` is required (rather than a bare `Provider`) because:
options: Trait objects are unsized and must sit behind a pointer — Box gives the indirection and ownership
Provider values exceed stack limits
dyn makes types cloneable
It queues providers in an async channel
explanation: Size limits aren't the reason; unsized-ness of dyn types is.
dyn has nothing to do with cloning (dyn Trait types aren't Clone by default).
Box is mere allocation; no channel semantics.

q: `fn summarize<T: Display>(items: &[T], max: usize) -> String` accepts:
options: Any slice whose element type implements Display — e.g. i32, String, ProviderStub with a Display impl
Only strings
Only integers
Any type, checked at runtime
explanation: The Display bound admits any Display type, including &str/String.
Integers are one admissible category, not the whole set.
Bounds are compile-time; there is no runtime checking.

q: `pub fn new(model_name: impl AsRef<str>) -> Self` (model.rs:103) is equivalent to:
options: `pub fn new<T: AsRef<str>>(model_name: T) -> Self`
`pub fn new(model_name: Box<dyn AsRef<str>>) -> Self`
`pub fn new(model_name: &str) -> Self`
A runtime duck-typed parameter
explanation: impl Trait in argument position is sugar for a generic bound, not a trait object.
&str is only one accepted type — the point is accepting String AND &str.
Rust never duck-types; the bound is static.

q: `MessageStream = Pin<Box<dyn Stream<Item = Result<(Option<Message>, Option<ProviderUsage>), ProviderError>> + Send>>` — which two facts are compile-time checked?
options: Each item has the exact Result<(Option<Message>, Option<ProviderUsage>), ProviderError> type, and the stream is Send
The stream length and its average item size
The provider's name and its API key
Stream items are deduplicated and sorted
explanation: Nothing about length/size is in the type.
Provider identity is not part of the stream type.
Ordering/dedup would be runtime behavior, not type-level facts.

q: Fix this compile error: `error[E0277]: the trait bound `ProviderStub: Named` is not satisfied` when calling `introduce(&stub)`. The fix:
options: Write `impl Named for ProviderStub` providing the required methods
Change the bound to `T: Display` only and delete Named
Annotate stub with `let mut`
Box the stub
explanation: Deleting the bound changes the function's contract instead of fulfilling it.
mut has nothing to do with trait impls.
Boxing doesn't magically implement Named.
